lesson.title: Watching a Capacitor Fill Up
lesson.summary: When a capacitor charges through a resistor toward a DC source, its voltage rises along a predictable exponential curve starting from its initial voltage and asymptotically approaching the source voltage.
lesson.body:
Picture an uncharged capacitor, an initial condition of zero volts across it, wired in series with a resistor to a battery through a switch. The moment the switch closes, current begins to flow, but the capacitor cannot accept charge instantly, its voltage can only rise gradually as charge accumulates on its plates. This process, RC charging, is one of the most common transient behaviors in electronics, showing up every time a capacitor is connected to a fresh source, from camera flash circuits to power-on reset networks.

The governing equations, derived from Kirchhoff's voltage law applied to the loop, are v_C(t) = Vs*(1 - e^(-t/RC)) for the capacitor voltage and i(t) = (Vs/R)*e^(-t/RC) for the current flowing through the resistor and into the capacitor. At t = 0, the exponential term equals 1, so v_C(0) = 0, matching the initial condition, and the current is at its maximum value Vs/R since the full source voltage initially appears across the resistor. As t grows large, the exponential term dies away, v_C approaches Vs, and the current approaches zero.

The reason this shape is exponential rather than, say, linear, comes directly from how much drive is left at each instant. The current charging the capacitor is proportional to the voltage difference remaining between the source and the capacitor, i = (Vs - v_C)/R. Early on, when v_C is still close to zero, that difference is large and current is high, so charge piles on quickly. As v_C climbs, the remaining difference shrinks, current drops, and charging slows down. The process continuously throttles itself, which is precisely the defining behavior of exponential growth toward a limit.

Consider a 9 V battery connected through R = 1 k ohm to an initially uncharged C = 1000 microfarad capacitor. The time constant is tau = RC = 1000 ohms times 0.001 farads, which is 1 second. At t = 1 second, one time constant has elapsed, so v_C = 9*(1 - e^-1) = 9*(1 - 0.3679) = 9*0.6321 = 5.69 V. At t = 3 seconds, three time constants have elapsed, so v_C = 9*(1 - e^-3) = 9*(1 - 0.0498) = 9*0.9502 = 8.55 V, close to the full 9 V. The initial current at t = 0 is Vs/R = 9V/1000 ohms = 9 mA, decaying exponentially from there with the same one second time constant.

Once the capacitor is fully charged, the energy stored in it is (1/2)*C*Vs^2 = 0.5*0.001 F*81 V^2 = 0.0405 J, or 40.5 mJ, exactly matching the capacitor energy storage relationship. What is less obvious is that the battery actually supplies twice that much energy overall, C*Vs^2 = 0.081 J, or 81 mJ, during the charging process. The other 40.5 mJ is dissipated as heat in the resistor, and remarkably this fifty-fifty split holds no matter what value of R is chosen, only the speed of charging changes, not the fraction of energy wasted. A smaller resistor charges the same capacitor to the same final energy much faster, but it still throws away exactly half of what the battery supplies, which is one reason very fast charging paths, like camera flash circuits, are engineered around this unavoidable loss rather than around eliminating it.
